blocks.text: Where an executive assistant's day goes

There is no public time study that measures what executive assistants do on a computer. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics does list the usual duties for secretaries and administrative assistants. The list includes scheduling appointments, updating event calendars, writing emails and memos, using spreadsheets and documents, and answering phones. Most of those tasks sit inside a few apps. For an EA, that usually means email, a calendar and a document.

The closest hard numbers come from executives. Fast Company reported on a Harvard Business School study by Porter and Nohria. It tracked CEOs at 27 billion-dollar companies for 13 weeks. Those CEOs attended an average of 37 meetings a week, and meetings took 72% of their work time. Email took 24%. An assistant often shapes that calendar and handles much of that inbox, so the pattern matters to your week.
Why email takes the largest share of the morning

Microsoft's Work Trend Index uses 2023 data from a 28-day period that ended in March 2023. On average, employees spent 57% of their time communicating and 43% creating. The heaviest 25% of email users spent 8.8 hours a week on email. Email took 15% of the time spent in Microsoft 365 apps. These are averages across all workers, not executive assistants. Use them as a starting point for your own week.

Run a simple test for one week. Keep a note of every block of time you spend in Outlook, Word and Excel. Sort each note into email, calendar, documents or other. Your own split tells you more than any industry average. Pay close attention to the first hour after you open email, because that is where the day often gets away from you.
What an AI assistant does in your day

Lazur covers five kinds of help for an EA. It explains what is on screen. It points at things you cannot find. It guides you through a task one click at a time. It handles everyday requests by voice, and it runs research in the background. It also drafts and types text, so you can work by voice when typing is slow.

Hold ⌥⌘ over an open message or calendar and ask what something means. Lazur answers out loud. Ask where a setting lives, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it on your screen. Ask how to do a task, and Lazur guides you one click at a time. It waits for each click before it moves on. You stay in control of the mouse and the send button.

Everyday requests work by voice. Ask for a timer, an Apple Reminders item, a Calendar event, a note, music or volume, an app or link to open, a web search, or a Shortcut. Start with a low-risk request, such as a reminder to chase a signed form. Dictation works differently. Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. Snippets, a personal dictionary and clipboard slots handle repeat work. Lazur also keeps a memory of what you asked and did, on your Mac.
Set up Outlook for Mac before you ask for help

Microsoft now makes the new Outlook the default on Mac. Microsoft's support page gives October 2026 as the end of support for legacy Outlook for Mac. Whether you keep support depends on your Microsoft 365, Office or Outlook license. Check which version your account runs before you follow any shortcut list. If your team needs the older app, the route is Help > Revert to Legacy Outlook. For a feature view, see [Lazur in Outlook](/apps/outlook).

Accounts do not carry over between the two versions. An account added in the new Outlook is not added to Legacy Outlook automatically, and the reverse is also true. If your executive has two mailboxes or a shared calendar, check each one in both versions. Check the account list before you assume a calendar is gone.

blocks.text: A morning inbox triage, step by step

Start with the list, not the first message. Open the inbox, hold ⌥⌘ and ask which messages need a decision today. Lazur reads the visible list and answers out loud. You still choose the order. Give triage a fixed slot at the start of the day, so it does not spill into lunch.

For a message that needs a reply, press ⌘R, then hold fn and dictate the answer. Lazur types clean text at the cursor. Read the draft once more before you press ⌘ Return. Dictation is quick, but it can drop a name or a figure. That mistake goes out under your executive's name.

For messages that can wait, set a reminder. Apple's Mail guide lists Remind Me in 1 Hour, Remind Me Tonight at 9:00 p.m., Remind Me Tomorrow at 8:00 a.m., and Remind Me Later with a custom date. Reminded messages return to the top of the inbox. For a thread that goes nowhere, choose Message > Mute in Apple Mail. Check notification rules in System Settings > Notifications. Ask Lazur to walk you through any of these if you cannot find them.
Calendar work: the 3-day view and suggested times

The new Outlook adds a 3-day calendar view. It also suggests meeting times based on attendee availability. Use the 3-day view when a full week is hard to read and a single day hides the pattern. Check suggested times before you send an invite. Suggestions only reflect the availability that Outlook can see.

A Working Elsewhere status tells colleagues where someone is working. Agree with your executive when to use it, and what it shows. Some blocks are private. Confirm them with your executive before you offer a time that looks open.

Time zones are an easy place to go wrong. Check the time zone on every invite that crosses a border. Ask Lazur to explain a time zone field if its label is unclear. Hold ⌥⌘ over the field, then ask what the setting controls. A correct time in the wrong zone still lands the executive in the wrong hour.
A worked example: booking a short call across time zones

items: Your executive is in New York and wants a short call with a partner in London this week.
Open Calendar with ⌘2 and look at the 3-day view for both calendars you can see.
Use a suggested time, then confirm the choice with your executive, who may hold a private block you cannot see.
Press ⌘N to start a new appointment. Set the time zone on the event itself, not only on your own computer.
Hold fn and dictate the invite note. Read it back, then press ⌘ Return to send it from the draft you checked.

blocks.text: Documents, templates and dictation in Word

Much of EA document work repeats. Agendas, minutes, letters and board papers follow the same shape. Build the template once in Word, then reuse it for each meeting. The Word guide for executive assistants covers templates, AutoText and Track Changes: [Word for executive assistants on Mac](/for/executive-assistants/word).

Dictation suits first drafts. Hold fn in Word and speak the minutes as the meeting moves. Then fix headings, lists and tables by hand. Dictation gives you text, not structure. Ask Lazur to explain a style if the heading you want is not obvious.

Snippets save the same sentence each week. Store your executive's sign-off, the dial-in block and the standard line for room bookings. Clipboard slots help when you move the same address or reference number between windows. Name each snippet clearly, so you can find it by voice.
When the request is a spreadsheet

Executives often ask for a travel total, an expense summary or a headcount for an event. Ask Lazur to explain a formula you do not recognize. Hold ⌥⌘ over the cell and ask what the SUM range covers. Check that every row uses the same currency and date format before you total anything. For a summary table, ask Lazur to guide you through a pivot table one click at a time. Step-by-step help is on [how to make a pivot table in Excel on Mac](/how-to/make-a-pivot-table-in-excel).
Research for trips, vendors and shortlists

Research runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs, through the Lazur for Chrome extension. It comes back with a summary and a report. Give it a clear brief. Name the city, the dates, the budget and the must-have features. A vague brief returns a vague report.
Check every price, opening time and cancellation rule on the vendor's own site before you book. Research gives you a shortlist. It does not replace the booking page or the contract.
Confidential material: follow your employer's rules first

blocks.title: Your employer's rules come first
blocks.text: Follow your employer's rules on confidential data before you use Lazur on any executive file. Lazur does not make your work compliant with any rule, and this page does not claim a compliance certification.

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers so they can answer. They are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Those are Lazur's product facts. They are not a promise about your company's policy, and your IT team sets that policy.

Before you hold ⌥⌘ over board papers, a contract, payroll or a personnel file, ask your executive and IT. Some firms block AI tools on managed Macs. Others allow them with conditions. Follow the rule you were given, even when a tool seems harmless.

A practical habit helps. Close or move sensitive windows off screen before you ask a question. Ask about the one message you need, not the whole inbox. Keep the question short, so the answer covers only what you need.
Mistakes EAs make with AI tools

items: Treating a draft as final. Lazur types text for you, but you read it and press send.
Trusting suggested times without checking your executive's private blocks.
Dictating names without checking them. Add people, venues and vendors to the personal dictionary first.
Keeping a decision only in a chat. Put it in the calendar, the minutes or the task list too.
Mixing up the new and legacy Outlook. Accounts do not carry between them.
Pasting a whole inbox thread into a question. Ask about one message at a time.

blocks.text: A one-week test before you rely on it

Pick one repeat task. Morning triage and the expense summary both work well as a first test. Use Lazur for that task every working day for one week. Time it before and after, and write the results in your own log. Do not rely on a vendor's figure for the time saved. Your own week is the data that counts.

faq.question: Is Lazur an AI assistant for executive assistants that works inside Outlook?
faq.answer: Lazur works next to Outlook, not inside it. It sees the screen while you hold ⌥⌘, explains what is on screen, points at buttons and guides you one click at a time. It is not a plugin or add-in for any app, and it does not operate Outlook for you.

faq.question: Can Lazur send email or accept invites for my executive?
faq.answer: No. Lazur drafts and types text, and it can walk you through the steps. You read every draft, check the recipients and press send yourself. Lazur does not click buttons for you.

faq.question: Does Lazur run on Windows?
faq.answer: No. Lazur runs on macOS, on both Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, but it is not available yet.

faq.question: What happens to my audio and screenshots?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer. Lazur's privacy facts say they are not stored, and content is never used to train AI models. Check your employer's rules before you use it on confidential files.

faq.question: Should I use Outlook or Apple Mail for this work?
faq.answer: Use whichever app your executive uses. Outlook for Mac has its own shortcuts and the new 3-day view. Apple Mail has its own Remind Me and Mute options. Keep one main mail app per mailbox, so you do not chase the same message in two places.

faq.question: Is legacy Outlook still supported on Mac?
faq.answer: Microsoft's support page gives October 2026 as the end of support for legacy Outlook for Mac. Support depends on your license. Ask IT which version your account should run before you change anything.

faq.question: How do I stop dictation from misspelling names?
faq.answer: Add the names to the personal dictionary before you dictate. Include executives, clients, venues and vendors. Check the first draft, especially the names, before you send it to anyone.

faq.question: Does the research feature book flights or hotels?
faq.answer: No. Research runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs and returns a summary and a report. You check prices, terms and availability on the vendor's site, and you book there.

faq.question: Does using Lazur make my work meet my industry's rules?
faq.answer: No tool makes work compliant on its own. Follow your employer's rules on confidential data, and ask IT before you use an AI tool on sensitive material. This page does not claim any compliance certification for Lazur.

painPoints.title: The inbox never empties
painPoints.text: Microsoft's 2023 data puts the heaviest 25% of email users at 8.8 hours a week on email. For an assistant, that time comes out of the rest of the day.

painPoints.title: Calendars that cross time zones
painPoints.text: Suggested times can look open while a private block sits behind them. Invites that cross a border can land on the wrong hour, so every one needs a check.

painPoints.title: Confidential files with no clear rules
painPoints.text: Board papers, payroll and personnel files sit on the same Mac as routine mail. Without a rule from your employer, every AI question becomes a guess.

painPoints.title: Outlook versions that do not match
painPoints.text: New Outlook is the default, and Microsoft's page gives October 2026 as the end of support for legacy Outlook. Accounts do not carry between the two.
